title: 401k Contribution Limits and Employer Matching
text: For the tax year 2026, the maximum individual contribution limit for traditional and Roth 401(k) accounts is $23,500. Catch-up contributions for individuals aged 50 and over allow an additional $7,500 per year. Employer matching contributions do not count towards the individual employee contribution limit, but are subject to the total annual additions limit under Section 415(c).

title: Capital Gains Tax Rules for Long-Term Investments
text: Long-term capital gains tax rates apply to assets held for more than one year prior to sale. The brackets for federal long-term capital gains tax are 0%, 15%, and 20%, depending on the filer's taxable income and marital filing status. Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) of 3.8% may also apply to high earners above threshold amounts.

title: Emergency Fund Allocation and High Yield Savings
text: Financial advisors generally recommend maintaining three to six months of essential living expenses in liquid, low-risk accounts such as High-Yield Savings Accounts (HYSA) or money market funds. This buffer protects individuals from liquidating investment portfolios during unexpected job losses or medical emergencies.

title: Roth IRA Income Limits and Backdoor Conversions
text: Direct contributions to a Roth IRA phase out for single filers with modified adjusted gross income between $146,000 and $161,000. Individuals earning above these thresholds often utilize the Backdoor Roth IRA strategy: making a non-deductible contribution to a Traditional IRA and subsequently converting it to a Roth IRA.
